books.title: Curiosity: Textbook of Science for Grade 8

source.method: chapter titles from the book's Contents page; topics from each chapter PDF's section headings

chapters.title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

topics.title: From Wonder to Investigation
objectives: Student can explain that investigating in science means asking focused questions, designing simple experiments and using observations to improve understanding
Student can explain what the root and the kite on the book's pages stand for: staying grounded in careful observation while letting ideas take flight
visualIdeas: a root at the bottom of a page and a kite soaring at the top, joined by a dotted line labelled observe - question - experiment

topics.title: Our Investigative Journey This Year
objectives: Student can name the big themes of the year, from microbes and health to forces, matter, light, the Moon and calendars, ecosystems and the Earth
Student can link one theme to the next, for example how pressure differences lead to winds and cyclones
visualIdeas: a winding road map with stops labelled microbes, health, electricity, forces, matter, light, Moon, ecosystems and Earth

topics.title: Investigating Why a Puri Puffs Up
objectives: Student can list what can be changed or controlled in a puri experiment (thickness, size, flour, oil temperature, way of dropping) and what can be observed or measured
Student can explain why only one thing should be changed at a time while the other conditions are kept the same
Student can describe systematic investigation as observing, experimenting, recording notes and asking new questions
visualIdeas: a table with columns things we change and things we observe, filled in for puris fried in oil of three temperatures

chapters.title: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye

topics.title: What Is a Cell?
objectives: Student can describe how onion peel and cheek cells are prepared and observed under a microscope
Student can name the basic parts of a cell (cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus) and state the function of each
Student can state that plant cells have a cell wall, plastids and a large vacuole, which animal cells usually lack
visualIdeas: side-by-side labelled diagrams of an onion peel cell and a human cheek cell
a brick wall next to a sheet of onion cells

topics.title: Variation in Shape and Structure of Cells
objectives: Student can compare the shapes of a muscle cell and a nerve cell
Student can explain how the shape of a cell suits its function, for example long branched nerve cells carrying messages
visualIdeas: a spindle-shaped muscle cell beside a long branched nerve cell with arrows showing a message travelling

topics.title: What Are the Levels of Organisation in the Body of a Living Organism?
objectives: Student can order the levels of organisation: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Student can explain that multicellular organisms begin as a single cell, the egg
visualIdeas: a staircase diagram from a single cell up to a whole organism

topics.title: What Are Microorganisms?
objectives: Student can define microorganisms as living beings too small to be seen with the naked eye
Student can name the groups seen in pond water and soil suspension: protozoa, algae, fungi and bacteria
Student can distinguish unicellular microbes like bacteria and Amoeba from multicellular ones like some fungi and algae
visualIdeas: a microscope view of a pond-water drop showing Amoeba, Paramecium and green algae

topics.title: How Are We Connected to Microbes?
objectives: Student can explain that microbes are found everywhere, in water, soil, air, food and inside our bodies
Student can explain why salt or sugar in pickles and murabbas stops microbes from growing
visualIdeas: a rotting orange with cotton-like mould beside a jar of pickle labelled salt and spices keep microbes away

topics.title: Key Players in Cleaning the Environment
objectives: Student can explain how fungi and bacteria decompose plant waste into nutrient-rich manure
Student can describe decomposition as returning nutrients to the soil
Student can state that some microbes living without oxygen break down waste and release biogas, mainly methane
visualIdeas: a compost pit cut-away showing peels turning into dark manure over three weeks

topics.title: Microorganisms and Food
objectives: Student can explain how yeast makes dough rise by releasing carbon dioxide during respiration
Student can explain how Lactobacillus turns warm milk into curd by producing lactic acid
Student can describe how Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes traps nitrogen from the air for plants
visualIdeas: two bowls of dough, one with yeast risen and bubbly, one without
root nodules of a cowpea plant with Rhizobium inside

topics.title: Amazing Microalgae: Tiny Helpers in Water
objectives: Student can state that microalgae make their own food using sunlight and produce more than half of Earth's oxygen
Student can give uses of microalgae such as Spirulina as food supplements, in cleaning water and in making biofuel
visualIdeas: a glass tank of green Spirulina being filtered through a fine cloth

topics.title: Why Is Cell Considered to Be a Basic Unit of Life?
objectives: Student can distinguish unicellular and multicellular organisms with examples
Student can state that bacteria have a nucleoid instead of a well-defined nucleus and that fungal cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts
visualIdeas: a bacterial cell with its nucleoid region labelled next to a yeast cell and a plant cell

topics.title: Health: Is It More Than Not Falling Sick?
objectives: Student can state the WHO definition of health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease
Student can explain from a case study how habits and surroundings affect a person's well-being
visualIdeas: three overlapping circles labelled physical, mental and social with health at the centre

topics.title: How Can We Stay Healthy?
objectives: Student can list good habits that keep us healthy and habits that harm health
Student can explain that health depends on both lifestyle and environment
visualIdeas: a two-column chart of healthy habits and harmful habits

topics.title: Maintain a Healthy Lifestyle
objectives: Student can describe a healthy lifestyle: balanced diet, physical activity, limited screen time, enough sleep, yoga or pranayama
Student can explain why tobacco, alcohol and addictive drugs must be refused
visualIdeas: a daily routine clock with meals, play, sleep and yoga marked

topics.title: Keep the Environment Clean
objectives: Student can explain why clean surroundings, air and water matter for health
Student can state that the Air Quality Index tells us how clean the air is
Student can explain that friendships and family time keep the mind healthy too
visualIdeas: a clean playground beside a littered one swarming with flies

topics.title: How Do We Know That We Are Unwell?
objectives: Student can distinguish a symptom (what we feel, like pain) from a sign (what can be seen or measured, like fever)
Student can give examples of symptoms and signs that show we are unwell
visualIdeas: a thermometer reading high temperature labelled sign next to a headache labelled symptom

topics.title: Diseases: What Are the Causes and Types?
objectives: Student can define a disease and a pathogen
Student can distinguish communicable diseases caused by pathogens from non-communicable diseases linked to lifestyle, diet and environment
visualIdeas: a sorting diagram with typhoid, dengue and flu on one side and diabetes, cancer and asthma on the other

topics.title: How Are Communicable Diseases Caused and Spread?
objectives: Student can describe how pathogens spread through air, direct and indirect contact, contaminated food and water, and vectors such as mosquitoes and houseflies
Student can suggest preventive steps for common communicable diseases such as cold, typhoid and malaria
visualIdeas: an infographic of an infected person passing germs by air, touch, food and a mosquito to a healthy person

topics.title: How Are Non-communicable Diseases Caused?
objectives: Student can explain that non-communicable diseases such as diabetes are linked to lifestyle, diet, environment and hormonal imbalance
Student can identify deficiency diseases and chronic diseases as kinds of non-communicable disease
visualIdeas: a lifestyle chart linking junk food, little exercise and overweight to diabetes

topics.title: How to Prevent and Control Diseases?
objectives: Student can explain how community sanitation reduces communicable diseases
Student can define immunity and explain how a vaccine trains the immune system to give acquired immunity
Student can describe how Edward Jenner's observations led to the first vaccine and to the eradication of smallpox
visualIdeas: a timeline from Jenner's cowpox experiment to smallpox eradication in 1979

topics.title: Treatment of Diseases
objectives: Student can explain that antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work against viruses
Student can describe Alexander Fleming's discovery of penicillin
Student can explain antibiotic resistance and why antibiotics must be taken only as prescribed, in the correct dose and duration
visualIdeas: a petri dish where mould stops bacteria from growing around it
a flow chart of how antibiotic-resistant bacteria spread in a community

topics.title: Does an Electric Current Have a Magnetic Effect?
objectives: Student can describe how a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle
Student can state that an electric current produces a magnetic field around a conductor
visualIdeas: a compass under a wire stretched between two nails, with the needle swinging when the switch is closed

topics.title: Electromagnets
objectives: Student can make an electromagnet by winding insulated wire around an iron nail and connecting it to a cell
Student can explain that a current-carrying coil behaves as a magnet only while current flows, and an iron core makes it stronger
Student can describe how cranes use lifting electromagnets to pick up and release iron and steel scrap
visualIdeas: a coil around a nail picking up paper clips with the circuit closed and dropping them when open
a crane magnet over a scrap yard

topics.title: Does a Current Carrying Wire Get Hot?
objectives: Student can describe how a nichrome wire gets hot when current flows through it
Student can define the heating effect of electric current and name appliances that use it
visualIdeas: a nichrome wire glowing between two nails beside an electric heater and iron

topics.title: How Does a Battery Generate Electricity?
objectives: Student can describe a Voltaic cell: two different metal electrodes dipped in an electrolyte
Student can explain that a chemical reaction in the cell produces electricity and that a cell is dead when its chemicals are used up
Student can recount how Galvani's frog-leg observation and Volta's idea led to the electric cell
visualIdeas: a simple Voltaic cell with two rods in a liquid lighting a lamp

topics.title: Dry Cells and Rechargeable Batteries
objectives: Student can describe the parts of a dry cell: zinc container as negative terminal, carbon rod as positive terminal, paste electrolyte
Student can explain that dry cells are single-use while rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused many times but slowly wear out
visualIdeas: a cut-away dry cell with its zinc case, carbon rod and paste labelled
rechargeable batteries in a phone, laptop and electric vehicle

topics.title: What Is a Force?
objectives: Student can define a force as a push or a pull on an object
Student can identify pushes and pulls in moving a box in different ways
visualIdeas: a box being pushed, pulled and lifted with arrows showing each force

topics.title: What Can a Force Do to the Objects on Which It Is Applied?
objectives: Student can explain that a force can change the speed or the direction of motion of an object
Student can explain that a force can change the shape of an object
visualIdeas: a bat changing a ball's direction and a hand squeezing a balloon

topics.title: Are Forces an Interaction Between Two or More Objects?
objectives: Student can explain that a force arises only when at least two objects interact
Student can state that the SI unit of force is the newton (N)
visualIdeas: a hand pushing a table with arrows on both the hand and the table

topics.title: Contact Forces
objectives: Student can define contact forces and give muscular force as an example
Student can explain friction as a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact and depends on the roughness of surfaces
visualIdeas: a box sliding on a floor with a friction arrow pointing against its motion
a bicycle stopping sooner on a rough road

topics.title: Non-contact Forces
objectives: Student can define non-contact forces and give magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational force as examples
Student can explain how rubbing gives objects static charges that attract small paper pieces
Student can state that gravitational force is always attractive and pulls all objects towards the Earth
visualIdeas: two ring magnets floating on a stick
a rubbed plastic scale attracting paper bits

topics.title: Weight and Its Measurement
objectives: Student can define weight as the force with which the Earth pulls an object, measured in newtons
Student can explain how a spring balance measures weight
Student can distinguish mass, which stays the same, from weight, which can change from place to place
visualIdeas: a spring balance stretching more for heavier objects

topics.title: Floating and Sinking
objectives: Student can explain upthrust (buoyant force) as the upward force a liquid applies on an object
Student can explain that an object sinks when gravity is greater than upthrust and floats when they are equal
Student can state Archimedes' principle
visualIdeas: a bottle pushed under water bouncing back with arrows for weight and upthrust

topics.title: Pressure: Force per Unit Area
objectives: Student can define pressure as force per unit area and state its SI unit, the pascal (N/m2)
Student can calculate pressure from a given force and area
Student can explain why broad bag straps feel comfortable and why a sharp knife cuts easily
visualIdeas: two school bags, one with broad straps and one with narrow straps, with the shoulder area shaded

topics.title: Pressure Exerted by Liquids
objectives: Student can explain from the balloon-and-pipe activity that liquids exert pressure that depends on the height of the liquid column
Student can explain why overhead water tanks are placed at a height
visualIdeas: two pipes of different widths filled to the same height with equally bulging balloons at their bottoms

topics.title: Pressure Exerted by Air
objectives: Student can explain that the atmosphere exerts pressure, called atmospheric pressure
Student can describe activities that show air pressing on surfaces
visualIdeas: an inverted paper plate held down by chart paper as air presses on it

topics.title: Formation of Wind
objectives: Student can explain that air moves from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure
Student can explain sea breeze and land breeze as winds caused by pressure differences over land and sea
Student can state that a bigger pressure difference makes the air move faster
visualIdeas: two balloons joined by a straw, air flowing from the inflated one to the other

topics.title: High-Speed Winds Result in Lowering of Air Pressure
objectives: Student can explain that fast-moving air has lower pressure
Student can explain why roofs can be blown off during high-speed winds
visualIdeas: air blown between two hanging balloons pulling them together
a roof lifting off a house in a storm

topics.title: Storms, Thunderstorms, and Lightning
objectives: Student can explain how rising warm moist air forms clouds and storms
Student can explain how charges build up in clouds and cause lightning
Student can state how lightning conductors protect buildings and what safety steps to take
visualIdeas: a thundercloud with plus and minus charges and a lightning bolt to a lightning conductor

topics.title: Cyclone
objectives: Student can describe how a cyclone forms over warm ocean water as a spinning low-pressure system
Student can identify the eye of a cyclone and explain why cyclones are dangerous
Student can state that the India Meteorological Department monitors cyclones and issues warnings
visualIdeas: a satellite-style spiral of clouds with the calm eye at the centre and pressure values decreasing inwards

topics.title: What Is Matter Composed of?
objectives: Student can explain from breaking and grinding chalk that matter is made of very small particles
Student can explain that grinding is a physical change in which only the size of the pieces changes
visualIdeas: a chalk stick broken into pieces, then powder, then a magnified speck

topics.title: What Decides Different States of Matter?
objectives: Student can explain that interparticle attractions hold the particles of matter together
Student can state that the strength of these attractions decides the physical state of a substance
Student can recall Acharya Kanad's idea of Parmanu
visualIdeas: particles connected by springs of different strengths for solid, liquid and gas

topics.title: Solid State
objectives: Student can explain why solids have a definite shape and volume
Student can explain that particles in solids are tightly packed, strongly attracted and only vibrate about fixed positions
visualIdeas: particles in a solid drawn in neat rows, each vibrating in place

topics.title: Liquid State
objectives: Student can explain from pouring water between containers that liquids have a fixed volume but no fixed shape
Student can explain that particles in liquids are less strongly attracted and can move about within the liquid
visualIdeas: 200 mL of water poured into three differently shaped containers

topics.title: Gaseous State
objectives: Student can explain from the smoke-in-gas-jar activity that gases have no fixed volume and fill the whole container
Student can explain that interparticle attractions in gases are negligible, so their particles move freely
visualIdeas: smoke spreading from one gas jar into an empty jar placed above it

topics.title: How Does the Interparticle Spacing Differ in the Three States of Matter?
objectives: Student can explain from the syringe activity why gases are easily compressed and liquids and solids are not
Student can compare interparticle spacing in solids, liquids and gases
visualIdeas: a sealed syringe of air being squeezed beside syringes of water and chalk

topics.title: How Particles Move in Different States of Matter?
objectives: Student can explain how potassium permanganate spreads through water because particles are always moving
Student can compare how freely particles move in solids, liquids and gases
visualIdeas: a crystal of potassium permanganate in water with pink streaks spreading out

chapters.title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures

topics.title: What Are Mixtures?
objectives: Student can define a mixture and its components
Student can distinguish uniform mixtures from non-uniform mixtures with examples
visualIdeas: a bowl of sprout salad beside a glass of sugar water

topics.title: Is Air a Mixture?
objectives: Student can explain that air is a uniform mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour
Student can describe a test that shows carbon dioxide is present in air
visualIdeas: a pie chart of the gases in air

topics.title: Types of Mixtures
objectives: Student can classify mixtures by the states of their components, such as gas in liquid or solid in liquid
Student can state that in science the components of a mixture must be pure substances
visualIdeas: a table of mixture types with soda water, vinegar, sand in water and seawater

topics.title: What Are Pure Substances?
objectives: Student can contrast the everyday meaning of pure (unadulterated) with the scientific meaning
Student can define a pure substance as one with only one kind of particle that cannot be separated by physical methods
visualIdeas: a packet labelled pure ghee with a question mark beside a beaker of distilled water

topics.title: What Are the Types of Pure Substances?
objectives: Student can describe how passing electricity through water gives hydrogen and oxygen
Student can state that pure substances are of two types, elements and compounds
visualIdeas: two inverted test tubes over electrodes collecting gas in a 2 to 1 ratio

topics.title: Elements
objectives: Student can define an element as a substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances
Student can explain that elements are made of atoms and that atoms of many elements combine to form molecules
Student can classify elements as metals and non-metals
visualIdeas: a hydrogen molecule and an oxygen molecule drawn as joined spheres

topics.title: Compounds
objectives: Student can define a compound as elements combined chemically in a fixed ratio with new properties
Student can explain from heating sugar that sugar is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
Student can distinguish a mixture of iron and sulfur from the compound formed by heating them
visualIdeas: iron filings and sulfur mixed on one watch glass and the black heated mass on another, with a magnet over each

topics.title: How Do We Use Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures?
objectives: Student can give everyday uses of elements, compounds and mixtures in buildings, medicines and fertilisers
Student can explain why alloys such as stainless steel are made
visualIdeas: a bridge, a medicine strip and a fertiliser bag each tagged element, compound or mixture

topics.title: What Are Minerals?
objectives: Student can define minerals as natural solid substances with a fixed chemical composition
Student can distinguish native minerals that are pure elements from minerals that are compounds
Student can give everyday products made from minerals, such as cement and talcum powder
visualIdeas: samples of quartz, calcite, mica and talc with the products made from them

chapters.title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions

topics.title: What Are Solute, Solvent, and Solution?
objectives: Student can define a solution as a uniform mixture and identify the solute and solvent in it
Student can identify the solute and solvent when two liquids are mixed
visualIdeas: salt crystals dissolving in water with particles spreading evenly

topics.title: How Much Solute Can a Fixed Amount of Solvent Dissolve?
objectives: Student can distinguish saturated and unsaturated solutions
Student can define solubility
visualIdeas: a glass of water with spoonfuls of salt added until some stays undissolved

topics.title: How Does Temperature Affect the Solubility of a Solute?
objectives: Student can explain from the baking soda activity that solids generally dissolve more in hotter water
Student can state that the solubility of most solids in a liquid increases as temperature increases
visualIdeas: a beaker of baking soda solution at 20, 50 and 70 degrees with less solid left each time

topics.title: Solubility of Gases
objectives: Student can explain that oxygen dissolves in water to a small extent and sustains aquatic life
Student can explain that gases dissolve less as temperature rises
visualIdeas: fish in cold and warm water with dissolved oxygen bubbles drawn more in the cold water

topics.title: Why Do Objects Float or Sink in Water?
objectives: Student can describe objects that float and sink in water, such as husk and rice
Student can explain that heaviness for the same size is described by density
visualIdeas: a wooden stick and an iron rod of the same size on a balance

topics.title: What Is Density?
objectives: Student can define density as mass per unit volume
Student can explain that density does not depend on shape or size but depends on temperature and pressure
visualIdeas: a crowded bus and an empty bus as a picture of high and low density

topics.title: Determination of Density: Measuring Mass and Volume
objectives: Student can measure mass with a digital balance after setting it to zero
Student can read a measuring cylinder and find its smallest division
Student can find the volume of an irregular solid by water displacement and calculate its density
visualIdeas: a stone lowered into a measuring cylinder with the water level rising

topics.title: Effect of Temperature and Pressure on Density
objectives: Student can explain why heating decreases density and why hot air balloons rise
Student can explain that pressure increases the density of gases but hardly affects solids and liquids
Student can explain why ice floats on water
visualIdeas: a hot air balloon rising
ice cubes floating in a glass of water

topics.title: What Are Spherical Mirrors?
objectives: Student can describe the images seen in the inner and outer surfaces of a shiny spoon
Student can define concave and convex mirrors as spherical mirrors that curve inwards and outwards
visualIdeas: a shiny spoon showing an inverted face on its inner side and a small upright face on its outer side

topics.title: What Are the Characteristics of Images Formed by Spherical Mirrors?
objectives: Student can describe how the image in a concave mirror changes as an object moves away
Student can state that a convex mirror always forms an erect, diminished image
Student can give uses of concave mirrors (torch reflectors, a dentist's mirror) and convex mirrors (side-view and road safety mirrors)
visualIdeas: a toy placed near and far from concave and convex mirrors with the images drawn

topics.title: What Are the Laws of Reflection?
objectives: Student can represent light as rays and identify the incident ray, reflected ray and normal
Student can state the two laws of reflection and verify them with a mirror and a comb slit
Student can explain that a concave mirror converges and a convex mirror diverges a beam of light
visualIdeas: a ray diagram on a plane mirror with equal angles of incidence and reflection marked

topics.title: What Is a Lens?
objectives: Student can identify convex and concave lenses
Student can describe the images formed by a convex lens and a concave lens
Student can explain that a convex lens converges and a concave lens diverges light
visualIdeas: a water drop magnifying letters
parallel rays meeting after a convex lens and spreading after a concave lens

topics.title: How Does the Moon's Appearance Change and Why?
objectives: Student can describe how to observe and record the Moon's shape over many days
Student can name the phases of the Moon and the waxing and waning periods (Shukla and Krishna Paksha)
visualIdeas: a strip of Moon sketches from new Moon to full Moon and back

topics.title: Locating the Moon
objectives: Student can explain how the Moon's position at sunrise changes from day to day
Student can explain why a waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset and a waning Moon at sunrise
visualIdeas: a sky dome at sunrise with the Moon in different positions on successive days

topics.title: Making Sense of Our Observations
objectives: Student can explain that the Moon shines by reflecting sunlight and only half of it is lit at any time
Student can explain the phases as the part of the lit half that faces the Earth as the Moon revolves
visualIdeas: a top view of the Sun, Earth and the Moon at eight positions with the lit half shaded

topics.title: How Did Calendars Come into Existence?
objectives: Student can explain how the day, the month and the year come from natural cycles
Student can explain why people needed calendars
visualIdeas: three cycles drawn as rings: day, Moon month and year of seasons

topics.title: Lunar Calendars
objectives: Student can explain that a lunar year has 12 lunar months of about 29.5 days, about 354 days in all
Student can explain why lunar months drift against the seasons
visualIdeas: a ring of 12 Moon phases falling 11 days short of a ring of seasons

topics.title: Solar Calendars
objectives: Student can explain that solar calendars such as the Gregorian calendar follow the seasons with 365 days
Student can explain why a leap year adds a day every four years
visualIdeas: a calendar page for February with a 29th day marked

topics.title: Luni-solar Calendars
objectives: Student can explain how an extra month (Adhika Maasa) every few years keeps a lunar calendar in step with the seasons
Student can name the months of Indian luni-solar calendars
visualIdeas: a timeline of lunar years with an extra month inserted every 2 to 3 years

topics.title: The Indian National Calendar
objectives: Student can state that the Indian National Calendar is a solar calendar of 365 days
Student can state when its year begins and name its first month, Chaitra
visualIdeas: a page of the national calendar showing Chaitra beginning on 22 March

topics.title: Are Festivals Related to Astronomical Phenomena?
objectives: Student can explain why festivals based on the Moon fall on different Gregorian dates each year
Student can contrast how festival dates shift in luni-solar and purely lunar calendars
visualIdeas: Diwali on a new Moon and Holi on a full Moon marked on two years' calendars

topics.title: Why Do We Launch Artificial Satellites in Space?
objectives: Student can distinguish the Moon, a natural satellite, from artificial satellites
Student can list uses of satellites in communication, navigation, weather monitoring and disaster management
visualIdeas: the Earth with satellites in orbit beaming signals to a phone and a weather map

topics.title: How Do We Experience and Interpret Our Surroundings?
objectives: Student can define a habitat and identify the living and non-living components of a habitat
Student can record observations of two habitats such as a pond and a tree
visualIdeas: a pond scene with living things circled green and non-living things circled blue

topics.title: Who All Live Together in Nature?
objectives: Student can define a population as a group of organisms of the same kind living in a place
Student can define a community as different populations living together
Student can count a population in a 1 m by 1 m area
visualIdeas: a quadrat on a school lawn with plants counted

topics.title: Does Every Organism in a Community Matter?
objectives: Student can explain from the pond study how fish, dragonflies, bees and plants are linked
Student can explain that removing one organism affects others in a community
visualIdeas: a pond with fish and one without, with arrows linking fish, dragonflies, bees and flowers

topics.title: What Are the Different Types of Interactions Among Organisms and their Surroundings?
objectives: Student can distinguish biotic and abiotic components and give examples of interactions between them
Student can define an ecosystem and name terrestrial and aquatic examples
Student can classify organisms as producers, consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) and decomposers
visualIdeas: a forest picture with arrows between sunlight, water, soil, plants and animals

topics.title: Who Eats Whom?
objectives: Student can draw a food chain for a grassland ecosystem
Student can explain how food chains link into a food web
Student can identify trophic levels in a food chain
visualIdeas: a grassland food web with grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hare and eagle

topics.title: What Happens to Waste in Nature?
objectives: Student can explain how decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter
Student can explain how decomposition returns nutrients to the soil
visualIdeas: mushrooms on a fallen log and beetles on dung with arrows to soil nutrients

topics.title: How Does One Change Lead to Another?
objectives: Student can trace how one change in an ecosystem, such as plants dying from pollution, leads to a chain of other changes
Student can explain from the frog-leg export case how removing frogs led to more pests and more pesticide use
visualIdeas: a chain of boxes: plants die, less oxygen, fish die, more insects, more pesticides

topics.title: How Do Interactions Maintain Balance in Ecosystems?
objectives: Student can explain how competition for resources keeps populations in check
Student can define mutualism, commensalism and parasitism with an example of each
visualIdeas: a bee on a flower, an orchid on a tree and a tick on a dog labelled with the relationship

topics.title: What Are the Benefits of an Ecosystem?
objectives: Student can list benefits humans get from forests and aquatic ecosystems
Student can explain why the Sundarbans mangroves are valuable and threatened
Student can give examples of human-made ecosystems such as farms, fish ponds and parks
visualIdeas: a map of the Sundarbans mangroves slowing storm waves

topics.title: How Do Healthy Ecosystems Serve Our Farms?
objectives: Student can explain how the Green Revolution raised food production and why its methods are now considered unsustainable
Student can explain how overusing pesticides and growing the same crop repeatedly degrades soil and harms natural predators of pests
visualIdeas: a field of a single crop beside a mixed field with earthworms and pollinators

chapters.title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet

topics.title: Why Is Earth a Unique Planet?
objectives: Student can explain that Earth is the only known planet where life exists
Student can explain that all life lives in a thin layer at the surface, like the skin of an apple
visualIdeas: an apple cut in half beside a cut-away Earth showing crust, mantle and core

topics.title: What Do the Planets of Our Solar System Look Like?
objectives: Student can name the eight planets in order from the Sun
Student can compare the small rocky planets with the large gaseous planets
visualIdeas: the eight planets in a row drawn to relative size

topics.title: Position of the Earth
objectives: Student can explain the habitable (Goldilocks) zone around a star
Student can explain why Earth's distance from the Sun keeps water liquid
visualIdeas: a star with too hot, just right and too cold rings and Earth in the middle ring

topics.title: Size of the Earth
objectives: Student can explain how Earth's nearly circular orbit keeps sunlight and heat nearly steady through the year
Student can explain why Earth's size and gravity let it hold an atmosphere
Student can explain how the ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet rays
visualIdeas: a small planet losing its air to space beside Earth holding its atmosphere

topics.title: Magnetic Field of the Earth
objectives: Student can explain that the Earth behaves like a giant magnet
Student can explain how Earth's magnetic field shields it from cosmic rays and the solar wind
visualIdeas: field lines around the Earth deflecting a stream of particles from the Sun

topics.title: Air, Water, and Sunlight
objectives: Student can explain how photosynthesis and respiration link plants and animals through oxygen and carbon dioxide
Student can explain how the mild greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for liquid water
visualIdeas: sunlight entering the atmosphere with some heat trapped and returned to the ground

topics.title: Soil, Rocks, and Minerals
objectives: Student can define the geosphere as the solid parts of the Earth
Student can explain how soil gets nutrients from broken-down rocks and remains of organisms
visualIdeas: a soil profile from topsoil down to bedrock

topics.title: Plants, Animals, and Microorganisms
objectives: Student can define the biosphere
Student can explain how producers, consumers and decomposers together support life
visualIdeas: the biosphere drawn as a band overlapping land, water and air

topics.title: The Importance of Balance
objectives: Student can explain how a change in one part of the Earth system, such as cutting a forest, affects the others
Student can explain why protecting air, water, soil and living things keeps Earth habitable
visualIdeas: a forest being cut with arrows to less rain, eroded soil and fewer animals

topics.title: What Keeps Life from Disappearing?
objectives: Student can explain that reproduction keeps each kind of organism going
Student can explain that genes carry the instructions passed from parents to offspring
visualIdeas: a cow with a calf and a cell drawn as an instruction manual

topics.title: Asexual Reproduction
objectives: Student can describe vegetative propagation from a leaf, stem or root
Student can give examples such as money plant, potato eyes, ginger, bamboo and sugarcane
visualIdeas: a money plant cutting growing roots in a glass of water

topics.title: Sexual Reproduction
objectives: Student can explain that two parents each make gametes carrying half the genetic material
Student can explain why offspring are not exact copies of either parent
visualIdeas: a male gamete and a female gamete joining to form a new cell with half the instructions from each

topics.title: What Are the Threats to Life on Earth?
objectives: Student can name the triple planetary crisis: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution
Student can explain how burning fossil fuels causes global warming
Student can describe actions that reduce these threats, such as renewable energy, global agreements like the Montreal Protocol and the Paris Agreement, and reusing and recycling
visualIdeas: a thermometer over the Earth with smokestacks, a felled forest and a polluted river
